standard.title: Geomorphological hazards
standard.description: the causes and impacts of a geomorphological hazard on people, places and environments, and the effects of responses
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain causes and impacts of atmospheric/hydrological hazards and community/government responses (AC9HG7K04). They now extend this cause-impact-response framework to geomorphological hazards (volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides, avalanches).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the causes and impacts of a geomorphological hazard on people, places and environments, and the effects of responses including prevention, mitigation and preparedness strategies.

nodes.label: Causes of geomorphological hazards
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the geomorphological causes of at least one hazard type.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the causes of one geomorphological hazard (volcanic eruption, earthquake, tsunami, landslide or avalanche).
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the geomorphological causes of selected hazard types, linking hazard type to the underlying processes — tectonic movement for earthquakes and tsunamis, volcanic pressure for eruptions, slope instability for landslides and avalanches.
wider: Compare the causal mechanisms of two hazard types (e.g., earthquake vs landslide), identifying what they share and what is distinct.
Investigate how the frequency and magnitude of hazard events relate to their geomorphological setting.
Examine how climate change is altering the frequency or distribution of geomorphological hazards (e.g., permafrost thaw and landslides).
nodes.hinge_reason: If students treat hazards as random events rather than outcomes of specific geomorphological processes, they cannot explain why particular places are at risk or why particular responses are effective — the core of Nodes 2 and 3.

response_modes.reason: Students need to connect geomorphological process knowledge from K01 to hazard causation. A process-to-hazard reasoning chain (plate boundary setting → stress type → hazard event) prevents treating hazard as an isolated phenomenon.

success_criteria: Names and explains the geomorphological cause(s) of at least one hazard type.
Links the hazard to an underlying geomorphological process (e.g., tectonic movement, slope instability).

nodes.label: Impacts on people, places and environments
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the environmental, economic and social impacts of a geomorphological hazard at the local scale.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two impacts (environmental, economic or social) of a named geomorphological hazard on a specific place.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the environmental (landscape change, biodiversity loss), economic (loss of industry, unemployment, infrastructure damage) and social (wellbeing, displacement, community vulnerability) impacts of a selected hazard at the local scale, using a specific case study.
wider: Compare impacts of the same hazard type in places with different levels of economic development and infrastructure.
Examine how vulnerability to hazard impacts is unevenly distributed within a community.
Investigate how human activities have heightened the impact of a hazard — land clearing increasing landslide risk, coastal development increasing tsunami impact.

response_modes.reason: Examining impacts across multiple dimensions (environmental, economic, social) and different community contexts prevents single-dimension impact analysis and builds the multi-factor reasoning students need for evaluating responses.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The triple-dimension impact framework (environmental, economic, social) applied comparatively across places with different vulnerability profiles is genuinely rich — wider students can develop nuanced arguments about differential hazard impact.
success_criteria: Describes at least two types of impact (environmental, economic or social) of a named hazard on a specific place.
Explains how the characteristics of the place (e.g., location, infrastructure, economic development) influence the scale of impacts.

nodes.label: Responses and their effects
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the effects of responses to geomorphological hazards, applying the principles of prevention, mitigation and preparedness.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain one response to a geomorphological hazard and its intended effect.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the principles of prevention, mitigation and preparedness as a framework for hazard response, applying them to a case study hazard and evaluating how the harmful effects of the hazard can be reduced. They reflect on how human activity has heightened vulnerability and how management strategies address this.
wider: Compare the effectiveness of prevention, mitigation and preparedness responses for different hazard types.
Examine how early warning systems have changed hazard outcomes in specific cases.
Investigate how community capacity and governance affect the quality of hazard response.

response_modes.reason: Evaluating responses requires students to bring together causal understanding (Node 1), impact analysis (Node 2) and knowledge of management principles into a coherent assessment of what works and why.

success_criteria: Applies at least one principle (prevention, mitigation or preparedness) to explain how the harmful effects of a named hazard can be reduced.
Explains the effects of a management response on people, places or environments.
